text: has been seen with fatty acid or dietary fish oil supplementation in active ulcerative colitis.17 Short-chain fatty acids have been proposed as a means of in- creasing butyrate levels, which may have a direct anti-inflamma- tory effect on the colon; butyrate enemas have shown benefit in ulcerative colitis.5,13,17 The use of a substrate (‘pre-biotic’) to de- liver short-chain fatty acids, or directly delivering probiotics to the intestine, have also been proposed.5,17 Glutamine has been suggested as being beneficial for epithelial integrity of the small intestine,1,16 although useful data are lacking.1,4,5 Much interest also surrounds the use of growth factors in enteral formulas, such as epidermal growth factor or transforming growth factor-β, which may have anti-inflammatory actions on the gut mucosa.7 Elimination diets, whereby foods are slowly reintroduced once remission has been achieved, aim to reduce relapse rates in Crohn’s disease, but the process is prolonged and complicated.1,3 In a study of patients with ulcerative colitis in remission, con- sumption of red and processed meat, protein, or alcohol in- creased the likelihood of relapse;18 these foods are rich sources of sulfur or sulfate, and sulfide toxicity may be important in the pathogenesis of ulcerative colitis.17 There is also some sugges- tion that titanium may be harmful in Crohn’s disease, and diets low in titanium have been advocated, with preliminary data sug- gesting a benefit.3 1.
